articles.title: Jensen is out. CUDA isn't. A Developer's Guide to Everything Nvidia Built
articles.description: Yesterday, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO, effective immediately. The stock fell as much as...
articles.body_html:
Yesterday, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO, effective immediately. The stock fell as much as 14% during the day before closing down 4.3%.

If you write code for a living, the stock drop is not the interesting part. The interesting part is that a single company, run by a single founder for 33 years, ended up owning the layer that almost every AI workload runs on. Your PyTorch training loop, your vLLM server and the model behind your coding assistant all sit on that layer.

So this post skips most of the boardroom drama and asks the developer questions. What did Nvidia actually invent? Why is CUDA so hard to leave? And does any of it change now that Huang is gone?

TL;DR

  • What happened: Huang resigned as president, CEO and director on November 12, 2026. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and Harvey C. Jones became Nvidia's first board chair. Nvidia gave no reason.
  • For developers, nothing changes this week. CUDA, cuDNN, NCCL, TensorRT and the Nemotron models keep shipping. Nvidia credits over 6 million developers with building on CUDA.
  • The key invention was making the GPU programmable: programmable shaders in 2001, then CUDA in 2006, put on every GeForce card, including cheap ones. That is why a grad student's gaming PC could train AlexNet in 2012.
  • The moat is software, not silicon. A rival chip has to replace compilers, PTX, libraries, profilers and framework support, not just match FLOPS.
  • Huang was one of open source's strongest allies in big tech. He agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.93 billion, co-wrote an industry letter defending open-weight models, and called DeepSeek-R1 "genuinely a gift to the world's AI industry." I counted 338 Nvidia engineers in the git history of open-source AI projects over the last 12 months, including DeepSeek's own kernel libraries.
  • Gaming paid for AI. Data center was $193.7B, about 90% of Nvidia's $215.9B in fiscal 2026 revenue. Gaming, the original business, was $16.0B.
  • You can research all of this with code. Every research example comes in two flavors: a fast Search call and a cited DeepResearch report, in JavaScript and Python.

Contents

  1. What actually happened
  2. Era 1: Graphics, and the chip that became programmable
  3. Era 2: CUDA, explained with code
  4. Era 3: AI factories
  5. Why the moat is software
  6. How gaming paid for AI
  7. Seven times Nvidia nearly failed
  8. The engineers behind the moat
  9. Jensen and open source: 338 engineers, counted
  10. Follow the money: who owns Nvidia, and who Nvidia owns
  11. Research Nvidia yourself, with code
  12. What changes for developers
  13. FAQ

What actually happened

Nvidia's board announced that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and director. It is the company's first CEO change since he co-founded it in 1993.

  • Interim CEO: Colette Kress, CFO since 2013. She keeps the CFO job too.
  • Board chair: Harvey C. Jones, the former Synopsys CEO, who has been on the board since 1993. Nvidia never had a chair before.
  • Reason: The release gives none. Press reports link the exit to a board review of Huang's personal conduct. Nvidia has not confirmed them, and its 8-K does not mention them.
  • Market: Shares closed down 4.34% at $166.19, about 30% below the October 6 record close.

That's the news. Now the engineering.

Era 1: Graphics, and the chip that became programmable

1993. Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem founded Nvidia to build 3D graphics chips for PCs.

1995: NV1, the wrong bet. NV1 rendered 3D with quadratic surfaces instead of the triangles the rest of the industry was standardizing on through Direct3D. Clever, and commercially wrong. Nvidia nearly died.

1997: RIVA 128, shipped without a prototype. Nvidia switched to triangles. With about six months of cash left, by Huang's account, it verified the RIVA 128 on a hardware emulator and sent the design straight to mass production. Huang has said he never held the chip before ordering it. If you've ever shipped to prod without a staging environment, imagine doing it with the whole company.

1999: GeForce 256 and the word "GPU." Nvidia marketed it as the world's first GPU. The real leap was hardware transform and lighting: moving per-vertex geometry math off the CPU. "First GPU" is Nvidia's label, and rivals dispute it, but the name stuck.

2001: GeForce 3 and programmable shaders. This is the one that matters for AI. Before GeForce 3, graphics chips ran a fixed pipeline. GeForce 3 let you write small programs, vertex shaders and pixel shaders, that ran for every vertex or pixel.

Once the hardware ran programs, researchers started abusing it for non-graphics math: encode your data as a texture, write a "shader" that's really a linear algebra kernel, read the result back as pixels. The hack got a name, GPGPU, and it was painful enough that someone had to build a real programming model.

2004: SLI. Two graphics cards sharing one game's rendering. A footnote now, but it was Nvidia's first product built on the idea that linking GPUs together is a feature. That idea comes back as NVLink.

Era 2: CUDA, explained with code

2006: G80 and CUDA. The GeForce 8800 (G80) replaced separate vertex and pixel units with unified shader cores that could run any program. With it, Nvidia announced CUDA: write GPU code in ordinary C, no texture tricks. The first public release followed in 2007. It was built by Ian Buck, who had created the Brook stream language for his Stanford PhD, and John Nickolls, who led the GPU computing architecture.

Twenty years later, the core ideas haven't changed.

The mental model

  • SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads). You write scalar code for one thread. The hardware runs it across thousands of threads in groups of 32 called warps.
  • A thread hierarchy. Threads form blocks, blocks form a grid. Blocks get scheduled onto streaming multiprocessors (SMs), so the same code scales from a laptop GPU to a data-center GPU with well over a hundred SMs.
  • An explicit memory hierarchy. Per-thread registers, fast per-block shared memory, and big but slow global memory. Most GPU performance work is moving data to the fast levels and keeping it there.
  • PTX, a virtual ISA. CUDA compiles to PTX, and the driver compiles PTX to each GPU's real instructions.

Hello world: one thread per element 

__global__ void add(const float* a, const float* b, float* c, int n) {
  int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;  // this thread's global index
  if (i < n) c[i] = a[i] + b[i];
}

// launch enough 256-thread blocks to cover n elements
add<<<(n + 255) / 256, 256>>>(a, b, c, n);

No loop. You describe what one thread does, and the launch configuration <<<blocks, threadsPerBlock>>> decides how many run.

Where it gets interesting: shared memory

The naive matrix multiply reads every element of A and B from global memory N times. The classic fix is tiling: each block loads a small tile of A and B into shared memory once, and every thread in the block reuses it.

#define TILE 16

__global__ void matmul(const float* A, const float* B, float* C, int N) {
  __shared__ float As[TILE][TILE];
  __shared__ float Bs[TILE][TILE];

  int row = blockIdx.y * TILE + threadIdx.y;
  int col = blockIdx.x * TILE + threadIdx.x;
  float acc = 0.0f;

  for (int t = 0; t < (N + TILE - 1) / TILE; ++t) {
    int aCol = t * TILE + threadIdx.x;
    int bRow = t * TILE + threadIdx.y;
    As[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = (row < N && aCol < N) ? A[row * N + aCol] : 0.0f;
    Bs[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = (bRow < N && col < N) ? B[bRow * N + col] : 0.0f;
    __syncthreads();  // wait until the whole tile is loaded

    for (int k = 0; k < TILE; ++k)
      acc += As[threadIdx.y][k] * Bs[k][threadIdx.x];
    __syncthreads();  // wait before overwriting the tile
  }

  if (row < N && col < N) C[row * N + col] = acc;
}

// dim3 block(TILE, TILE);
// dim3 grid((N + TILE - 1) / TILE, (N + TILE - 1) / TILE);
// matmul<<<grid, block>>>(A, B, C, N);

Each global value is now loaded N / TILE times instead of N times, a 16x cut in global-memory reads for this tile size. Production libraries like cuBLAS and CUTLASS go much further (register tiling, async copies, Tensor Cores), which is exactly why almost nobody writes their own matmul. That gap between "correct kernel" and "fast kernel" is a big part of the moat.

PTX: why your old binaries still run

When you compile with nvcc, you can embed PTX alongside machine code for a specific GPU:

nvcc -gencode arch=compute_70,code=sm_70 \
     -gencode arch=compute_70,code=compute_70 \
     kernel.cu -o app

code=sm_70 is native machine code for Volta. code=compute_70 embeds the PTX itself, which the driver can JIT-compile for GPUs that didn't exist when you built the binary. Nearly two decades of forward compatibility is one of the most underrated reasons teams stay on CUDA.

The business decision behind the code

The API wasn't the bold part. Putting CUDA on every GeForce card was. It cost die area and margin on products whose buyers just wanted to play games, and Wall Street questioned it for years. But it meant every student with a gaming PC owned a parallel computer they could program.

2010: Fermi added ECC memory, a real L1/L2 cache hierarchy and much faster FP64, which made GPUs acceptable to supercomputer centers.

2012: AlexNet. Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton trained a deep CNN on two GeForce GTX 580 gaming cards and won ImageNet with about 15% top-5 error against roughly 26% for the runner-up. Deep learning had been waiting for cheap parallel compute. CUDA on gaming GPUs supplied it.

2014: cuDNN. Nvidia packaged hand-tuned convolutions, pooling and activations into a library, and every framework adopted it. That became the pattern: find the hot loop in a new field, write the fastest library for it, and give it away to sell hardware.

2016: P100, NVLink, DGX-1. HBM2 memory, the first NVLink (a GPU-to-GPU link far faster than PCIe) and an eight-GPU "AI supercomputer in a box." Huang hand-delivered the first DGX-1 to a small non-profit called OpenAI.

Era 3: AI factories

2017: Volta and Tensor Cores. Neural nets spend most of their time multiplying matrices. Tensor Cores do a small matrix multiply-accumulate (a 4x4 block in the first generation) in mixed precision every clock. Every Nvidia data-center GPU since has them.

2018: Turing, RT cores and DLSS. Real-time ray tracing for games, plus DLSS: render at lower resolution, upscale with a neural network on the Tensor Cores. AI sold gaming, and gaming funded AI.

2020: A100 and Mellanox. Multi-Instance GPU slices one A100 into up to seven isolated GPUs. Nvidia also closed its $6.9B purchase of Mellanox, the InfiniBand leader. Training a large model is as much a networking problem as a compute problem, and Nvidia now owned both.

2021: Grace. An Arm-based data-center CPU built to feed GPUs over NVLink-C2C. (Nvidia doesn't make gaming CPUs; your gaming PC's CPU is Intel or AMD.)

2022: H100 and the Transformer Engine. It switches parts of a transformer to FP8 and back where accuracy needs it, roughly doubling effective throughput on the workload that was about to take over. Nvidia announced it in March 2022, eight months before ChatGPT launched.

2024: Blackwell and GB200 NVL72. Two dies acting as one GPU (208 billion transistors), FP4 support, and a liquid-cooled rack of 36 Grace CPUs and 72 Blackwell GPUs joined by NVLink switches at 130 TB/s, behaving like one giant GPU. The unit of compute became the rack.

2023 to 2026: Inference software and open models. TensorRT-LLM for fast LLM inference, Dynamo for spreading inference across GPUs, NIM containers for deployment, and the Nemotron 3 open models (December 2025) with a hybrid mixture-of-experts design and open training data. Reports put Nvidia's open-model commitment at roughly $26 billion over five years. Same playbook as cuDNN: make the best free software for your hardware.

Next: Nvidia says Vera Rubin is in production with partner systems from the second half of 2026, Rubin Ultra in 2027 and Feynman in 2028. Those are company plans, and details keep shifting.

Why the moat is software

AMD's MI-series GPUs, Google's TPUs, Amazon's Trainium and plenty of startups all post strong benchmark numbers. Raw FLOPS isn't the problem. Everything above the chip is.

  • Libraries: cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL (the collective-communication library that lets thousands of GPUs average gradients), CUTLASS, cuFFT, RAPIDS.
  • Tools: nvcc, PTX, and the Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute profilers you open when a kernel is mysteriously slow.
  • Frameworks: PyTorch, vLLM and SGLang treat CUDA as their primary backend, and other chips usually get support later. Even JAX, built for Google's TPUs, runs on Nvidia GPUs through CUDA.
  • People: at GTC 2026, marking 20 years of CUDA, Nvidia credited over 6 million developers.

You feel this in one line of PyTorch:

import torch

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = torch.nn.Linear(1024, 1024).to(device)

The device string is literally "cuda". A rival doesn't have to beat a chip. It has to make that line, and the millions of kernels, configs and tutorials behind it, work on day one.

How gaming paid for AI

Nvidia didn't pivot from gaming to AI. Gaming funded AI for about 15 years.

  1. Gamers bought GeForce cards in the tens of millions.
  2. Those profits funded GPU R&D.
  3. CUDA turned every card into a programmable parallel computer.
  4. Researchers used cheap gaming GPUs, and AlexNet proved the approach.
  5. TensorFlow and PyTorch were built CUDA-first because that's where the researchers were.
  6. AI labs bought data-center GPUs by the rack, funding the next generation.
Fiscal year Total revenue Gaming Data center
FY2016 $5.0B $2.8B (56%) $0.34B (7%)
FY2023 $27.0B $9.1B (34%) $15.0B (56%)
FY2026 $215.9B $16.0B (7%) $193.7B (90%)

Source: Nvidia 10-K filings. Fiscal 2026 ended January 25, 2026.

Gaming didn't shrink. It grew 41% in fiscal 2026. Data center just grew far faster, and networking alone passed $31 billion.

Seven times Nvidia nearly failed

Nvidia's history looks like a straight line up only in hindsight. Early backer Mark Stevens has said that "between 1993 and 1997 we almost went bankrupt three times".

  1. 1995, NV1 flops. Huang asked Sega to drop Nvidia's console contract but turn the rest into an investment. That $5 million kept Nvidia alive.
  2. 1997, RIVA 128. Months of cash, an emulator instead of prototypes, and a hit.
  3. 2002 to 2003, Xbox. A pricing fight with Microsoft went to arbitration. The next Xbox went to ATI, and the Xbox had been 15% to 20% of sales.
  4. 2008, "bumpgate." A packaging flaw killed laptop GPUs. The stock fell 31% in a day, and Nvidia took a $196M charge.
  5. 2018, crypto hangover. Mining demand vanished and the stock fell 18.8% in a day.
  6. 2022, Arm deal dies. Regulatory opposition in the US, UK and EU sank the $40B deal. Nvidia took a $1.36B charge and built its own Arm CPU anyway.
  7. 2025 to 2026, China. Export rules shut Nvidia out of China's data centers, with a $4.5B H20 charge.

The pattern: cut losses on the committed path, keep investing in the next architecture.

I didn't build this list by hand. You can reproduce it two ways with Valyu. Install the SDK first: npm install valyu-js (or pip install valyu for Python).

Search returns ranked sources in seconds, for about $0.003 a call. Good for checking one fact:

import { Valyu } from "valyu-js";

const valyu = new Valyu(process.env.VALYU_API_KEY);

const res = await valyu.search(
  "NVIDIA near bankruptcy history NV1 Sega investment RIVA 128",
  { maxNumResults: 5 }
);

for (const r of res.results) {
  console.log(r.title, r.url);
}

DeepResearch reads dozens of sources and writes the report for you. This list started as a Valyu DeepResearch report: one API call, 36 sources (SEC filings, Huang's interviews, news archives back to 2002), a cited report in under five minutes for about $0.16. I then checked every figure against its source:

import { Valyu } from "valyu-js";

const valyu = new Valyu(process.env.VALYU_API_KEY);

const task = await valyu.deepresearch.create({
  query:
    "Every time NVIDIA nearly failed, from its 1993 founding to 2026: " +
    "what happened, what decision saved it, and the outcome. Cite primary sources.",
  mode: "fast", // instant | fast | standard | heavy | max
});

const report = await valyu.deepresearch.wait(task.deepresearch_id);
console.log(report.output);  // markdown report with citations
console.log(report.sources); // every source it used

Swap the company name and you have a post-mortem generator for any company you're curious about. You can get an API key here.

The Engineers behind the moat

Nvidia gets reduced to one person. These people built the parts developers touch:

  • Ian Buck created CUDA and now runs Nvidia's hyperscale and HPC business.
  • John Nickolls co-architected CUDA, including its software-managed shared memory, and co-wrote the 2008 paper "Scalable Parallel Programming with CUDA." He died in 2011, far less known than the platform he helped build.
  • David Kirk, chief scientist from 1997 to 2009, founded NVIDIA Research.
  • Bill Dally left the chair of Stanford's CS department to become chief scientist in 2009. Under him, research produced NVLink and RT cores. He recalls Huang first rejecting NVLink with "we don't do networking." He also had Bryan Catanzaro port Google Brain's cat-recognition network to GPUs, which by Dally's account "ran faster on 48 GPUs than on 16,000 CPUs." That code became cuDNN.
  • Chris Malachowsky, co-founder, led hardware engineering and is still at Nvidia as an NVIDIA Fellow.

Jensen and open source: 338 engineers, counted

On the day Huang resigned, TechCrunch wrote that the open-source community "just lost one of its strongest advocates." For a company that sells proprietary chips and a closed-source CUDA, that sounds odd. The record says otherwise.

What Huang did for open source

  • 2022: open GPU kernel modules. Nvidia published its Linux GPU kernel modules under a dual GPL/MIT license, starting with the R515 driver (announcement).
  • 2025: praising DeepSeek. After DeepSeek-R1 knocked Nvidia's stock down in January 2025, Huang told analysts the bigger story was that DeepSeek had "open sourced a world-class reasoning AI model". In May he called R1 "genuinely a gift to the world's AI industry."
  • 2026: defending open weights in Washington. He co-wrote an open letter, signed by 25 companies including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Palantir, urging the US government not to over-restrict open-weight models (TechCrunch). He also defended Chinese open models directly: "Open-source models that are excellent should be used."
  • 2026: buying Hugging Face. On September 3, Nvidia agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.93 billion. In his announcement, Huang wrote that Nvidia compute "will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face." The deal had not closed when he resigned.
  • Nvidia's own output. Nvidia says it is the largest contributor of open models and data on Hugging Face, with more than 500 models and 250 datasets, plus more than 1,000 open-source projects on GitHub. That includes NeMo, Megatron-LM, TensorRT-LLM, Dynamo, Triton Inference Server, CUTLASS and NCCL. Even Nvidia's NIM containers for LLMs run on vLLM or SGLang underneath.

It's not pure idealism. More teams training and serving their own models means more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs that are now designing their own chips. Either way, the open ecosystem got a lot out of it. AI researcher Nathan Lambert put the worry bluntly: losing Huang as CEO would be "very very bad for the open model cause in the US." One Nvidia insider told TechCrunch they don't expect the leadership change to affect Nemotron development.

Counting the engineers

Press releases are one thing. Commits are better evidence. I cloned ten major open-source AI repos and counted distinct @nvidia.com addresses in each commit's author, Co-authored-by and Signed-off-by lines over the 12 months to November 13, 2026.

Project What it is Nvidia engineers (12 months) Commits with an Nvidia name
vLLM LLM serving 185 732
SGLang LLM serving 96 479
PyTorch Training framework 43 619
llama.cpp Local inference 20 289
JAX Google's ML framework 18 73
Transformers Hugging Face models 10 12
All 10 repos (incl. DeepSeek's) 338 2,200+

Treat this as a floor. Plenty of Nvidia engineers commit with personal or GitHub no-reply emails, which this method can't see. You can run it yourself on any repo:

git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm
cd vllm
git log --since=2025-11-13 \
  --format='Author: <%ae>%n%(trailers:key=Co-authored-by,key=Signed-off-by)' \
  | grep -io '[a-z0-9._+-]*@nvidia\.com' | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sort -u | wc -l
# 185

The --filter=blob:none --no-checkout clone pulls commit history without file contents, so even PyTorch downloads in minutes.

Nvidia engineers inside DeepSeek's code

The most interesting commits aren't in Nvidia's repos. They're in DeepSeek's. DeepSeek open-sourced the low-level libraries behind its models, and Nvidia engineers have contributed to three of them (all-time counts):

  • DeepEP, the expert-parallel communication library for mixture-of-experts models: 10 Nvidia engineers. Their commits added CPU-assisted IBGDA networking support and support for upstream NVSHMEM packages, added the UE8M0 data format and documented a Hybrid-EP branch.
  • DeepGEMM, DeepSeek's FP8 matrix-multiply kernels: 2 Nvidia engineers, with fixes for Blackwell (SM100), NVRTC compilation, support back to CUDA 12.3 and prebuilt wheels.
  • FlashMLA, the multi-head latent attention kernels: 3 Nvidia engineers, with SM100 attention fixes and a fix for sequences longer than a million tokens.

DeepSeek's 3FS file system had no Nvidia commits.

Nvidia also works on the models themselves:

  • It publishes FP4 versions of DeepSeek-R1, such as nvidia/DeepSeek-R1-NVFP4, quantized with TensorRT Model Optimizer to run on Blackwell. Its TensorRT-LLM team published how it tuned DeepSeek-R1 latency on B200.
  • It shipped day-0 Blackwell support for DeepSeek V4.
  • Its OpenReasoning-Nemotron models are distilled from DeepSeek-R1-0528 into Alibaba's Qwen2.5 base models, and released openly.

Research it yourself

Search, for quick sources:

from valyu import Valyu

valyu = Valyu()  # reads VALYU_API_KEY from the environment
res = valyu.search(
    "NVIDIA engineers contributions to DeepSeek DeepEP DeepGEMM open source",
    max_num_results=5,
)
for r in res.results:
    print(r.title, r.url)

DeepResearch, for a cited write-up:

from valyu import Valyu

valyu = Valyu()

task = valyu.deepresearch.create(
    query=(
        "How have NVIDIA engineers contributed to open-source AI software and "
        "open-weight models, including PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and "
        "DeepSeek's DeepEP, DeepGEMM and FlashMLA? Cite commits, blog posts and releases."
    ),
    mode="fast",  # instant | fast | standard | heavy | max
)

report = valyu.deepresearch.wait(task.deepresearch_id)
print(report.output)   # markdown report with citations
print(report.sources)  # the sources it used

Follow the money: who owns Nvidia, and who Nvidia owns

Huang never controlled Nvidia. He held 3.58% (870.6 million shares in the 2026 proxy), and Nvidia has no dual-class shares, so there were no super-voting rights like Zuckerberg has at Meta. BlackRock (8.0%) and Vanguard (about 8.5% across two entities) each own more than he does.

The stock plan made engineers rich. Stacked yearly RSU grants plus a 15%-discount employee stock purchase plan, applied to a share price up roughly 200x since early 2016. One share bought at the 1999 IPO for $12 is now 480 shares, about $79,800. Turnover was 3.7% in fiscal 2026, which helps explain why the people who know CUDA's internals tend to stay.

And Nvidia owns a slice of your toolchain. Huang has no verified personal angel investments, but under him Nvidia joined about 260 startup funding rounds: 177 directly and 83 through its NVentures arm (Crunchbase, February 2026). That list includes the tools and models a lot of you use daily: Anysphere (Cursor), Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and more. Its check into OpenAI went from a reported $100M in October 2024 to $30B in February 2026.

Research Nvidia yourself, with code

Everything above is checkable. Ownership is in SEC filings, and the inventions left a patent trail. Both are painful to dig through by hand, so here's how I did it with Valyu's Search API.

Find the patent behind Tensor Cores 

import { Valyu } from "valyu-js";

const valyu = new Valyu(process.env.VALYU_API_KEY);

const res = await valyu.search(
  "NVIDIA tensor core mixed precision matrix multiply accumulate",
  {
    includedSources: ["valyu/valyu-patents", "valyu/valyu-patents-epo"],
    maxNumResults: 5,
  }
);

for (const p of res.results) {
  console.log(p.title, p.metadata?.filing_date, p.url);
}

The top hit is US 10,338,919, "Generalized acceleration of matrix multiply accumulate operations," assigned to NVIDIA, filed on November 29, 2017 and granted in July 2019. The same search surfaced two of its continuations, US 10,884,734 (granted 2021) and US 12,321,743 (granted 2025). The query cost $0.04. Try "NVLink", "unified shader architecture" or "transformer engine FP8" next.

Or have DeepResearch trace the whole patent family

Search finds the patents. DeepResearch reads them and explains how the claims evolved:

import { Valyu } from "valyu-js";

const valyu = new Valyu(process.env.VALYU_API_KEY);

const task = await valyu.deepresearch.create({
  query:
    "Trace NVIDIA's Tensor Core patent family: the original filing, " +
    "its continuations, what each one claims, and how the claims changed " +
    "over time. Cite each patent number.",
  mode: "fast", // instant | fast | standard | heavy | max
});

const report = await valyu.deepresearch.wait(task.deepresearch_id);
console.log(report.output);  // markdown report with citations
console.log(report.sources); // every source it used

When I ran it, the report traced the whole chain: the 2017 original plus seven continuations granted between 2021 and 2025. Each one keeps the same title but narrows the claims, from a broad matrix multiply-accumulate method to specific processor designs and data types such as FP16 and signed or unsigned integers. That's how a company keeps one invention covered as its hardware changes.

Pull the ownership table from SEC filings 

from valyu import Valyu

valyu = Valyu()  # reads VALYU_API_KEY from the environment
filings = valyu.search(
    "NVIDIA proxy beneficial ownership table directors executive officers",
    included_sources=["valyu/valyu-sec-filings"],
    max_num_results=3,
)
for f in filings.results:
    print(f.title, f.url)

That returns the "Security Ownership" section from Nvidia's last three proxy statements in one call, for $0.036. Put them side by side and you find something no single filing shows: Huang's stake fell from 934.6M split-adjusted shares (2024) to 922.9M (2025) to 870.6M (2026).

Tip: name the document type in your query ("proxy", "10-K", "8-K"). It matches the right section much more reliably. More in the query-writing guide.

Or let DeepResearch do the comparison 

from valyu import Valyu

valyu = Valyu()

task = valyu.deepresearch.create(
    query=(
        "Using NVIDIA's DEF 14A proxy statements, compare the beneficial ownership "
        "of directors and executive officers across the last three years. "
        "Show how Jensen Huang's stake changed and cite each filing."
    ),
    mode="fast",  # instant | fast | standard | heavy | max
)

report = valyu.deepresearch.wait(task.deepresearch_id)
print(report.output)   # markdown report with citations
print(report.sources)  # the sources it used

If you'd rather click than code, the same searches run on the Valyu platform.

What changes for developers

This week: nothing. CUDA, the libraries and the Nemotron models keep shipping. The board says the roadmap continues, and Vera Rubin is already in production. Chip roadmaps are set years ahead.

Over the next year, watch three things:

  1. Who the next CEO is. Huang made the CUDA bet, the Mellanox bet and the open-model bet, each years before it paid off. An operator CEO might protect margins instead of making the next ten-year bet.
  2. Whether senior engineers stay. Unvested stock ties a lot of people to Nvidia, and their grants now ride on a new strategy. The engineers behind CUDA and the libraries are the real moat.
  3. How hard buyers hedge. AMD and Broadcom rose on the news. Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium and custom accelerators already exist, and a leadership gap gives big buyers another reason to make their code portable.

The bottom line: the moat in this story was built by thousands of engineers over 20 years. It's in PTX, cuDNN, NCCL and six million developers' muscle memory, and it doesn't resign with the CEO. The open question is whether Nvidia can keep placing the next decade-long bet without the person who placed all the previous ones.

Not investment advice.

FAQ

What did Nvidia invent?
The biggest inventions: the GeForce 256, which Nvidia marketed as the first GPU (1999); programmable shaders in GeForce 3 (2001); CUDA (2006); NVLink and the DGX system (2016); Tensor Cores (2017); RT cores and DLSS (2018); Multi-Instance GPU (2020); the Transformer Engine with FP8 (2022); and the GB200 NVL72 rack-scale system (2024). Through Mellanox it also became the leading InfiniBand supplier.

What is CUDA, and why is it so hard to replace?
CUDA is Nvidia's platform for running general-purpose code on GPUs, introduced in 2006. You write code for one thread and the GPU runs it across thousands. It's hard to replace because two decades of libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL), tools, framework backends and about 6 million developers are built on it.

Who created CUDA?
Ian Buck created CUDA after joining Nvidia in 2004, building on Brook, the GPU language from his Stanford PhD. John Nickolls co-architected it. Nvidia announced CUDA with the GeForce 8800 (G80) in November 2006, and the first public release followed in 2007.

Does Nvidia make gaming CPUs?
No. GeForce cards are GPUs. The CPU in a gaming PC usually comes from Intel or AMD. Nvidia does make data-center CPUs, Grace and its successor Vera, designed to work alongside its GPUs.

Did Jensen Huang support open source?
Yes, strongly. Under Huang, Nvidia open-sourced its Linux GPU kernel modules (2022), released more than 1,000 open-source projects and 500+ open models, praised DeepSeek-R1's open release, and agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.93 billion in September 2026. In 2026 he co-wrote an industry letter urging Washington not to over-restrict open-weight models.

How many Nvidia engineers contribute to open source?
At least 338 distinct @nvidia.com engineers appear in the commit history of ten major open-source AI repos (vLLM, SGLang, PyTorch, llama.cpp, JAX, Transformers and DeepSeek's DeepEP, DeepGEMM, FlashMLA and 3FS) between November 13, 2025 and November 13, 2026. That is a floor, because engineers who commit with personal emails are not counted.

Do Nvidia engineers contribute to DeepSeek?
Yes. Nvidia engineers have commits in DeepSeek's open-source DeepEP (10 engineers), DeepGEMM (2) and FlashMLA (3) repositories, covering networking, Blackwell support and build fixes. Nvidia also publishes FP4 DeepSeek-R1 checkpoints, shipped day-0 Blackwell support for DeepSeek V4, and distilled DeepSeek-R1-0528 into its OpenReasoning-Nemotron models.

Why did Jensen Huang resign?
Nvidia's announcement gives no reason. Press reports link the exit to a board review of his personal conduct, and Nvidia has not confirmed them.

Who is Nvidia's CEO now?
Colette Kress, CFO since 2013, is interim CEO and remains CFO. The board is searching for a permanent CEO. Harvey C. Jones is the first board chair.

Does this affect CUDA or PyTorch?
Not in the short term. CUDA, its libraries and framework support keep shipping, and the product roadmap is set years ahead. The longer-term questions are leadership, engineer retention and how fast buyers diversify to other chips.

Over to you: have you tried moving a real workload off CUDA, to ROCm, TPUs, Trainium or anything else? What broke first? Tell me in the comments.

A longer version of this post, with the full shareholder table, the board and the employee wealth breakdown, is on Medium.

articles.body_html:
Quando estava construindo o Downshift, precisei entender melhor como o Claude Code gastava contexto e escolhia os modelos dos subagentes. Eu vinha de uma dor bem concreta: pagava o plano Pro e, em poucos dias de trabalho, já tinha esgotado o limite semanal. Queria entender o que estava consumindo tanto e onde fazia sentido otimizar.

É como trabalhar com outro dev: passar a tarefa é só o começo. A gente também combina os limites, divide o que pode andar em paralelo e confere se a entrega atende ao que foi pedido. Com agentes, precisamos ainda decidir qual modelo usar, quanto esforço dedicar e o que vale carregar na conversa.

A decisão que vale levar para o próximo projeto é esta: escolher capacidade conforme o problema e dar ao agente uma forma concreta de verificar a entrega. Vamos aplicar isso a uma correção de API, com comandos e configurações que você pode adaptar.

1. Escolha modelo e esforço antes de aumentar o prompt

Imagine que POST /pedidos recebe {"quantidade": -1} e retorna 201 Created. Neste exemplo didático, o contrato exige quantidade positiva e prevê 400 Bad Request para esse caso. Precisamos corrigir a validação e manter a criação de pedidos válidos funcionando.

Para começar, confira três coisas diferentes:

Configuração O que significa Como conferir
Versão do Claude Code O programa instalado e os recursos disponíveis claude --version no terminal
Modelo Quem recebe e resolve a tarefa /model na sessão
Effort O esforço solicitado para raciocinar e executar /effort status na sessão

O material que inspirou este artigo destaca uma mudança específica: Opus 5.5 em medium iguala ou supera Opus 5 em high nas avaliações de código e trabalho de conhecimento da Anthropic. Carregar a configuração antiga para a versão nova pode deixar de ser uma boa escolha. Isso não é um benchmark do nosso projeto. Fonte: configuração de modelos e esforço.

Na documentação consultada em 12/11/2026, opus, sonnet e haiku resolvem para a família 5.5 na API da Anthropic. Outros provedores podem usar versões anteriores. Opus 5.5 exige Claude Code v2.1.280+, Sonnet 5.5 v2.1.284+ e Haiku 5.5 v2.1.293+. Para repetir uma comparação, registre o ID completo. Tabela por provedor.

Modelo e effort não são a mesma alavanca. O modelo define a capacidade; o esforço influencia quanto trabalho ele dedica ao turno, incluindo investigação e verificação. Mais esforço pode gerar mais tokens e espera. Não define um teto fixo de gasto. Explicação da Anthropic.

Na API do exemplo, eu usaria esta referência inicial, como hipótese para testar:

Situação Combinação inicial Motivo
Extrair campos e localizar consumidores conhecidos Haiku 5.5, medium Pesquisa delimitada, com retorno fácil de conferir
Corrigir validação com teste reproduzível Sonnet 5.5, medium Implementação com escopo e aceite claros
Investigar regressão com hipóteses concorrentes Opus 5.5, medium Diagnóstico exige cruzar evidências
Diagnóstico continua inconclusivo Comparar Opus 5.5 em medium e high Verificar se aprofundar melhora a solução

Na prática: se o teste já mostra que falta uma validação, Sonnet em medium é meu ponto de partida. Se o erro só aparece com duas requisições simultâneas, preciso investigar concorrência: aí testaria Opus, começando em medium. A incerteza da tarefa orienta a escolha.

Para abrir a sessão de implementação no terminal:

claude --model claude-sonnet-5-5 --effort medium

A escala da família 5.5 inclui low, medium, high, xhigh e max. Comece no padrão e aumente quando houver uma lacuna concreta na investigação. Para mudar, use /effort high; a seleção direta salva a preferência para o modelo. A variável CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL pode prevalecer e políticas da organização podem limitar o nível. Níveis e precedência.

Um detalhe de versão: no Claude Code v2.1.311+, ultrathink tem tratamento específico e pode elevar aquele turno a xhigh nos casos suportados. think e think hard são texto comum. A afirmação de que todas essas palavras perderam efeito ficou desatualizada. Semântica atual.

2. Dê um contrato de trabalho e um mapa curto

Em vez de começar com “analise profundamente e siga todas as boas práticas”, descreva o comportamento que precisa mudar:

Tarefa: POST /pedidos aceita quantidade -1 e retorna 201.
O contrato prevê 400 para quantidade não positiva; corrija a validação.
Primeiro, escreva um teste que reproduza a falha.

Limites: preserve os campos e os status previstos no contrato.
Pedidos válidos devem continuar retornando 201.
Não altere o esquema do banco.

Pronto: o teste falha antes da correção e passa depois;
as verificações relevantes passam e o diff pode ser revisado.
Se faltar informação sobre o contrato, apresente a dúvida antes de alterá-lo.

Isso dá ao agente uma tarefa executável e permite ao revisor conferir o resultado. Para experimentar sem um repositório pronto, salve o arquivo abaixo como pedidos_test.go. Ele contém o handler e os testes e usa apenas a biblioteca padrão do Go.

Exemplo completo: handler e testes em um arquivo 
package pedidos

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "strings"
    "testing"
)

func novoHandler(criar func()) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        var pedido struct {
            Quantidade int `json:"quantidade"`
        }
        if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&pedido); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "JSON inválido", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        // Correção: rejeitar antes do efeito colateral.
        if pedido.Quantidade <= 0 {
            http.Error(w, "quantidade deve ser positiva", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        criar()
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
    })
}

func TestCriarPedido(t *testing.T) {
    casos := []struct {
        nome, corpo      string
        status, criacoes int
    }{
        {"negativa", `{"quantidade":-1}`, 400, 0},
        {"zero", `{"quantidade":0}`, 400, 0},
        {"positiva", `{"quantidade":1}`, 201, 1},
    }
    for _, caso := range casos {
        t.Run(caso.nome, func(t *testing.T) {
            criadas := 0
            handler := novoHandler(func() { criadas++ })
            req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "/pedidos",
                strings.NewReader(caso.corpo))
            req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
            res := httptest.NewRecorder()
            handler.ServeHTTP(res, req)
            if res.Code != caso.status {
                t.Errorf("status: esperado %d, recebido %d", caso.status, res.Code)
            }
            if criadas != caso.criacoes {
                t.Errorf("criações: esperado %d, recebido %d", caso.criacoes, criadas)
            }
        })
    }
}

Execute no diretório onde salvou o arquivo:

go test -v pedidos_test.go

Para reproduzir o bug, remova temporariamente o bloco if pedido.Quantidade <= 0 e repita o comando. Os casos negativo e zero falham: recebem 201 e criam um pedido. Restaure a validação e rode novamente: os três casos passam. O teste confere tanto o status quanto o efeito colateral; devolver 400 depois de criar o pedido não resolveria o problema.

Conferi esse ciclo localmente para o artigo: sem a validação, dois casos falharam; com ela, os três passaram. É uma demonstração de comportamento HTTP, sem banco, autenticação ou servidor de produção. Em uma API real, mantenha os demais campos válidos para a falha acontecer pelo motivo que está testando.

O CLAUDE.md complementa esse pedido com o que vale para o projeto: comando de testes, convenções próprias e caminhos das regras. Não precisa recontar o funcionamento de Go ou copiar toda a documentação. A recomendação oficial é mantê-lo abaixo de 200 linhas. Imports @ carregam conteúdo; dividir um documento usando imports não elimina seu custo de contexto. Use ponteiros e regras por caminho quando fizer sentido. Memória e regras.

O Plan Mode continua útil para explorar uma mudança ampla antes de editar. Ele controla a etapa de trabalho e as ferramentas disponíveis; não aumenta o effort. Para esse bug delimitado, eu começaria pelo teste. Boas práticas.

3. Separe a pesquisa quando ela atrapalhar a correção

Se descobrir os consumidores exigir ler dezenas de arquivos, essa exploração pode ocupar a conversa inteira. Um subagente consegue pesquisar em contexto separado e devolver as evidências relevantes. Para uma busca curta, abrir outro agente pode acrescentar mais coordenação do que benefício.

Uma definição didática em .claude/agents/contratos-api.md:

---
name: contratos-api
description: Investiga consumidores de endpoints sem editar arquivos.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: haiku
effort: medium
---
Identifique campos, status e consumidores do endpoint solicitado.
Retorne arquivo e linha de cada evidência e declare as lacunas.

Peça: “Use contratos-api para investigar os consumidores deste endpoint; retorne o contrato observado e o que não conseguiu confirmar.”

Um retorno útil nesse cenário seria: “O contrato prevê 400 para quantidade não positiva e 201 para pedido válido. Localizei o consumidor web, mas não confirmei o comportamento do aplicativo mobile.” É uma resposta ilustrativa; numa execução real, ela precisa trazer arquivo e linha das evidências. Essa lacuna deve continuar visível na revisão.

Aqui, a escolha do modelo é explícita e as ferramentas permitem apenas leitura. O alias acompanha o provedor; fixe o ID completo quando precisar reproduzir um teste. O subagente também consome cota: preservar a conversa principal não significa eliminar esse consumo. Configuração de subagentes.

Também não suponha que o effort será sempre herdado. Sem configuração própria, no mesmo modelo ele acompanha a seleção da sessão; em outro modelo, essa seleção não se aplica. Declare effort quando precisar controlar essa escolha e confira o modelo em /tasks. Regras de esforço.

4. Faça o agente demonstrar que terminou

Na nossa API, uma entrega útil mostra três evidências: o teste reproduziu o problema, passou após a correção e as verificações relevantes foram executadas sobre o código final. “Revise duas vezes” não define nenhuma dessas provas.

Para continuar automaticamente até uma condição de término, /goal aceita um objetivo como:

/goal Corrigir o endpoint e incluir o teste de regressão.
Prova: executar as verificações do projeto e trazer à conversa
os comandos, códigos de saída e resumo dos resultados.
Preservar contrato público e esquema do banco.
Após 15 turnos, parar e relatar o bloqueio se não houver prova.

O avaliador de /goal lê a conversa; não abre arquivos nem executa comandos por conta própria. Por isso, a prova precisa aparecer no histórico. O limite de turnos escrito no objetivo é interpretado pelo avaliador, não um teto rígido de execução. O recurso também consome tokens e não muda as permissões. Funcionamento de /goal.

Na revisão, eu pediria: o nome dos testes executados, o resultado antes e depois e se o código mudou após a última execução. Isso permite conferir a entrega sem aceitar um “agora funciona” como prova.

Limites críticos precisam de controles além do texto. Um hook de comando PreToolUse pode bloquear uma chamada antes da execução com código de saída 2 e explicar o motivo em stderr. Sua eficácia depende das ações que ele consegue identificar e interceptar; um filtro de comandos não protege sozinho todos os acessos ao banco. Contrato dos hooks.

É a aplicação prática de guias e sensores em harness engineering, por Birgitta Böckeler: instruções orientam; controles e verificações dão retorno sobre o que aconteceu.

Como conferir consumo sem confundir tokens com a conta

Ao concluir uma tentativa, abra /usage. O bloco de sessão apresenta tokens por modelo, incluindo entrada, saída, leitura e escrita de cache, além de duração e custo estimado. No Pro, o valor em dólares não é uma cobrança adicional: a tela também mostra os limites do plano. Para faturamento de API, confira o provedor. Referência de consumo.

Na comparação, salve uma linha por tentativa:

tarefa | modelo/versão | effort | passou? | tokens por categoria |
custo estimado | duração | tentativas | intervenção humana

Use o mesmo estado inicial do código, prompt, testes, skills e ferramentas. Abra sessões novas, alterne a ordem das configurações e registre o estado do cache; não compare uma sessão já aquecida com outra fria como se fossem equivalentes. Repita os casos antes de concluir que houve ganho.

Inclua as falhas na conta: some o consumo de todas as tentativas de uma configuração e divida pelas entregas aceitas. Se nenhuma passou, não há custo por entrega aceita a reportar. Mantenha tokens de cache separados: um token lido do cache e um token de saída não têm o mesmo preço. A ocupação da janela de contexto também não representa todo o consumo acumulado.

O que essa comparação mostrou no Downshift

Foi essa distinção que precisei levar para o Downshift. No estudo de 21/10/2026, a bateria teve 46 execuções com tarefas mecânicas e delegação obrigatória:

Configuração Aceitas Tokens por execução aceita
opusplan nativo 10 de 11 2,00 milhões
opusplan com roteamento do Downshift 12 de 12 1,52 milhão

O relatório registra 24,1% menos tokens por execução aceita, contando as falhas no consumo do grupo. O compactador estava desligado nos dois grupos comparados; essa diferença é do experimento de roteamento. O intervalo de 95% foi amplo: de 2,1% a 46,7%. Mais de 98% dos tokens eram de cache. Portanto, esse percentual não significa a mesma redução na fatura ou aumento do limite semanal do Pro.

É um resultado histórico do roteamento usado naquele experimento, anterior à mudança de arquitetura O8, como ressalva o README atual. Não comprova o efeito da implementação atual, nem se estende a tarefas gerais. O aprendizado aplicável aqui é medir a entrega aceita e identificar de onde vem a diferença antes de anunciar economia.

Para uma skill que já existe, compare tarefas equivalentes com e sem ela. O estudo independente skill-placebo, com 450 execuções no Opus 5.5, reforça esse cuidado: nenhum dos nove pacotes demonstrou custo menor que a condição sem skill naquela amostra. Isso não decide o valor da sua skill; mostra por que precisamos medir.

O ganho que eu buscaria é conseguir responder, ao revisar a entrega: por que usamos essa capacidade, o que o agente pôde fazer e qual evidência mostra que a mudança funciona? Com essas respostas, fica mais fácil ajustar o consumo sem trocar qualidade por uma sessão aparentemente barata.

Referências

  • Vídeo que inspirou a seleção dos temas — IA em 6 minutos.
  • Modelos, versões e esforço e explicação do mecanismo.
  • Memória e CLAUDE.md, boas práticas e subagentes.
  • Hooks, /goal e medição de consumo.
  • Downshift: estudo controlado de tarefas mecânicas, 21/10/2026.
  • Skill-placebo: método e resultados.
  • Harness engineering — Birgitta Böckeler.

articles.title: The Question I Never Asked
articles.description: The word landed in the middle of a Tuesday meeting, in the big room, the one where the air...
articles.body_html:
The word landed in the middle of a Tuesday meeting, in the big room, the one where the air conditioner hummed like it was thinking about quitting.

We were redesigning the sync service, and the lead said, "We'll go with eventual consistency on this one," and kept talking like he had just said something normal, like "we'll use Postgres" or "let's order lunch." Everyone around the table made small agreeing noises. I made one too. Then I nodded.

I had a whole technique for the nod by then, though I didn't know it yet. It was slow, two beats, chin down and up, with a little pen tap at the end, as if the nod had a full stop. It said: yes, of course, eventual consistency, the obvious choice, carry on. It said all of that in half a second, and none of it was true. I had no idea what eventual consistency was. I had heard the words before, the way you hear a song on the radio and can hum the chorus but not name the band. Consistency. Eventually. Something about databases agreeing with each other, probably. Eventually.

The meeting moved on. I wrote the words in my notebook and put a star next to them, the way you star a message you plan to read later and never do.

Afterwards, back at my desk, I googled it: "eventual consistency simple explanation." The first result was a blog post with a diagram of two databases holding hands. The second was a Wikipedia page that used the word "convergence" in the first sentence and lost me by the third. The third was a forum answer that began, "Actually, it's quite simple," and then ran for nine hundred words. I read all three. I closed all three. I understood it the way you understand a joke someone explains to you: the words went in, the meaning waved at me from a distance and kept walking.

So I did what I always did. I nodded harder.

That is the part nobody tells you about the nod. It works. That is the problem. Nobody checks. Meetings move fast, and a confident nod is a tiny green light. The lead saw mine and kept going. The next week, someone said "idempotency" and I nodded at that too, and wrote it in the notebook with another star. The week after that it was "backpressure." By March the notebook had eleven stars. Eleven words I had nodded at and never looked up. My notebook started to look like a star chart. I told myself I would look them all up on Friday. I never looked them up on Friday. Friday was for the things I had already put off on Thursday.

I started rehearsing explanations in the shower. That was the lowest point, probably, though I didn't know it then. I would stand there with the water going cold and explain eventual consistency to the tiles, in a confident voice, using words like "convergence" that I had stolen from the Wikipedia page. The tiles were a generous audience. They never asked follow-up questions.

The dread came later, and it came in a specific shape. It was not the fear of being found out in general. It was the fear of one sentence: "Salam, what do you think?" The lead said it the way leads do, casually, eyes scanning the room for someone who had been quiet. I had been quiet because I was busy nodding. I started volunteering to take the meeting notes, because a man writing things down has a reason to look at his notebook instead of at the lead. My notes were excellent. My notes were the best notes in the team. They were also a hiding place with bullet points.

Once, I nearly asked. The lead said "backpressure" and I actually opened my mouth, and then a senior engineer asked a question about the queue depth, a real question with numbers in it, and the moment closed like a door. I told myself the timing was wrong. The timing was always wrong.

The worst part was that I was not stupid. I knew that, in the way you know things at 2 a.m. and forget by 10. I could build the thing. I could read the code. I just could not say the words out loud without feeling like someone would ask me to keep going, and then I would be standing there with an empty bucket and a long way to the well. So I kept the bucket hidden and nodded.

Then, one Thursday, the bucket came out anyway.

It was a sprint review. The product manager asked whether users would see their updates straight away, and I heard myself say, "It's eventually consistent, so, you know, a few seconds, max." I said it the way I had heard other people say it: lightly, confidently, like a man describing his own kitchen. And then Maya, the senior dev, who was refilling her water bottle by the window, said, "Eventually doesn't have a max. That's the whole deal. It could be a second. It could be an hour, if something's stuck. Eventually is a promise without a deadline."

She said it the way you tell someone the lift is out of order. No smile of victory, no pause for the room to enjoy it. She just said it, and sat down, and the meeting went on. Nobody laughed. Nobody even looked at me the way I had spent a year imagining people would look at me. The product manager said "ah, okay, good to know," and wrote something down. The floor did not open. The sky did not fall. I sat there with my face burning and a strange feeling underneath the burning, like the moment after you take a plaster off and find the skin underneath is fine.

That evening I looked it up properly. Not the frantic googling of before. I read one article slowly, with the notebook open, and I wrote down what it meant in my own words, the way you would explain it to a friend: the system promises the copies will agree, but it does not promise when. I wrote that sentence twice. Then I looked up idempotency, and backpressure, and three other stars. It took forty minutes. Forty minutes, for a year of dread. I did the maths on that and decided not to do the maths on that. Then I closed the laptop and went for a walk, and I felt something I had not felt in a year of meetings. I felt like I had put down a bag I had forgotten I was carrying.

The next week, the lead said "idempotency" again. I heard myself say, "Sorry — quick one. When you say idempotent, you mean we can run the same request twice and nothing bad happens, right?"

The room did something I did not expect. Two people visibly relaxed, the way people relax when someone else says the thing they were thinking. One of them laughed and said, "Thank god. I was going to google that tonight." And Maya, from her corner, said, "I have a bookmark folder for this stuff. I look it up every single time. Eleven years in, and I still check."

Eleven years. She had been doing this eleven years, and she still checked. I thought about my notebook full of stars. I thought about the hiding place with bullet points. I almost laughed, right there in the meeting, and I had to turn it into a cough.

After that, the questions got easier, the way anything gets easier once you have done it once and survived. I asked about backpressure. I asked about the retry policy. Once I asked a question and the answer was something I actually knew, and I felt foolish for about four seconds, and then I forgot about it, because nobody else remembered it either. I asked a question in a meeting with the client, and the client said, "Good question, I was wondering that too," and I wrote that down in the notebook as well, without a star, because some things you do not need to look up later.

A year later, almost to the week, I was in the same big room, the same air conditioner still thinking about quitting, and the lead said "eventual consistency" again. This time I was the one who had been in the room the longest. And across the table, a new engineer, first week, did the nod. The slow nod. Two beats. Chin down and up. And then the pen tap, the little full stop. I knew that nod the way you know your own handwriting. I still have the notebook. The stars are still there.

After the meeting I caught him by the kettle. "Hey," I said. "Eventual consistency. It just means the copies promise to agree, but nobody promises when. That's all it is."

He looked at me, and his shoulders did something I recognised. They went down, half an inch, like he had put down a bag.

"Oh," he said. "That's it?"

"That's it," I said.

He nodded. And so did I. This time I knew what I was nodding at.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Wild Shift Devlog #3: SIGSEGV incoming
articles.description: Third update on The Debugger 0x03: Wild Shift, my GitHub Game Off 2026 entry (theme: SHIFT). Devlog...
articles.body_html:
Third update on The Debugger 0x03: Wild Shift, my GitHub Game Off 2026 entry (theme: SHIFT). Devlog #1 covered the register and the shift, Devlog #2 the first two bosses. This post is a mirror of the third devlog on itch.io. You can also play the current build in the browser on the game page.

The last bug is in. Since the last devlog The Debugger 0x03: Wild Shift got its final boss, two new combos, an intro and an ending. For the first time the run has a beginning, a middle and a return 0;.

Two new combos (Epic 6)

With all four bits in the register ([A, D, L, N]) there are new pairs to read, and two of them are now real combos:

  • Ghost Echo (L→N). Echo, then Null Dodge: you turn intangible and leave a decoy where you started. For two seconds the boss aims at the decoy instead of you. If an attack hits the decoy while the boss's weak window is L→N, the boss is Patched. You don't hit the boss, you let it hit itself.
  • Dereference (N→A). Press K while your Null Dodge is still active and you thrust 3 tiles forward, intangible, piercing everything in the line. It's the strongest single hit in the game, and with Patched plus Clean Catch it goes from 30 to 68. Press it too late and you get a plain slash instead: dereference after free is undefined behaviour.

Segfault: the bug that touches memory it shouldn't

The final boss is Segfault, a glitch dragon of ▓▒░#@! glyphs, 1000 HP, crawling back and forth across the top third of the arena. The sky comment reads // HACK: do not read past this line, and nobody listened.

Its three phases want the three combos you've been collecting: D→L (Echo Dash through the claw), then N→A (Dereference), then L→N (Ghost Echo). Every combo you learned in the run has a job here.

  • Access Violation. The claw's arc and the exact rectangle it will sweep are drawn for half a second before it swipes. Step out of the box and you're fine. Stay in it and you learn something.
  • Corrupt Memory. 8 to 12 floor tiles get marked ░, then turn into ▓ hazards for four seconds. Walking onto one costs 1 HP. The marks are always shown for a full second first: no damage you didn't see coming.
  • Core Dump (phase 3). The whole floor becomes a checkerboard. Half of it is safe (·), half of it isn't, and you have three seconds to dance on the right squares.


Segfault in the top band, phase 2, with Corrupt Memory's ▓ tiles spread over the floor.


Access Violation's tell: the claw arc and the box it's about to sweep.

SIGSEGV: the theme turns against you

This is the one I was waiting for. In phases 2 and 3 the screen gets a red border and the sky row flashes SIGSEGV incoming. One second later the boss rotates your register by two slots. [A, D, L, N] becomes [L, N, A, D], and the combo you had under your fingers is now somewhere else.

It's always telegraphed, it never lands on top of another attack, and it's followed by a long recovery (90 frames, 150 if Breakpoint is cut) so you have time to read the new window and punish. Red is reserved for exactly two things in this game: Breakpoint and SIGSEGV.


SIGSEGV incoming: red border, and the register is still [A, D, L, N]...


...one second later it's [L, N, A, D], and J→K is suddenly Ghost Echo.

Reserved Write

In phase 3 the four reserved cells under the register start blinking. Then the boss writes a garbage bit ? into your ring for ten seconds. ? does nothing: its solo action is a NOP and it forms no combo with anything. Five bits, one of them useless, and the windows keep sliding. When it expires your register goes back exactly as it was.


Reserved Write: the register reads ADLN? and the ? A window is dead weight.

Beat it and the dragon collapses into the line it should have been: if (idx < len) buf[idx] = val;.

A beginning and a return

  • Intro. Three quick panels, about 8 seconds: 2 a.m., stuck on a bug; squeeze the duck (QUACK); the screen tears into glyphs and you land in The Clearing. The duck hands you your first two bits: "Quack. Explain the bug to me. Use these." Any key skips it.
  • Ending. The next morning, back at the desk. The four reserved cells light up one by one until the register reads 0xFF, a commit types itself out (c0ffee1 fix: wild shift), and the duck gets the last word: "Quack. Works on your machine now." A real run also shows your clear time and how many hits you took, then the credits.


The ending: the register finally full at 0xFF, and the commit that fixes everything.

The credits list my own font, Wildshift8, and the duck's voice, mumble-speech, my own library. The audio line still says TBD: music comes next.

(Yes, the "FIGHT 3 / boss index 2" text in the middle of the arena is still the scene-flow placeholder. It goes away in polish.)

Every word in its place

The last story of the epic was a text audit. Every line of game text now lives in data and is checked against the design doc by a test: exactly 10 duck lines (the budget I set at the start), 3 fixed lines (one per boss) and 3 sky comments. If someone adds an 11th duck line, the build fails. The duck is chatty, but within limits.

How it's made

Same as before: I'm the director and the playtester, AI agents (Claude) write the code from specs I approve with the BMAD Method, and every story is a pull request with code review and automated tests. The test suite went from 95 to 112 test files. Everything is public in the GitHub repo.

The plan had Epic 6 for November 22–25. It was merged on November 13, so the whole game is now playable start to finish with more than two weeks left before the deadline.

Next up

The game is complete but quiet. Next is the part that makes it feel finished: music, the final sound pass, save and resume, a browser and performance check, and a full-run playtest with real people. If you want to help break it, the current build is playable right here on this page.

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: Git 2.56's history-drop Is 40-77x Faster Than Rebase — I Built It and Got 6x
articles.description: Git 2.56 shipped on September 28 with a new experimental command, git history drop, and the headline...
articles.body_html:
Git 2.56 shipped on September 28 with a new experimental command, git history drop, and the headline number travelling with it is 40 to 77 times faster than rebase. I built Git 2.56 from source this morning, ran the same comparison on my own machine, and got 6 times faster.

Six is not forty. But the story behind the gap is more useful than either number, because the new command's speed is nearly identical on both machines. It's the old way that's wildly different. And that tells you exactly when the new command matters.

Building Git 2.56 first

Git 2.56.0 isn't in Ubuntu's repositories yet, so I built it from the tagged source, the same starting point as the original comparison. It took three tries, and the failures are worth knowing about if you try this yourself.

First failure: curl/curl.h missing. This machine has no libcurl development headers, so the build died on the HTTP code. Second failure: cargo: not found. Git 2.56's default build wants Rust for one of its libraries. Both are fixable without installing anything, because the Makefile has switches for exactly this:

make -j2 NO_CURL=1 NO_RUST=1 prefix=/tmp/git-256 all

Rust is still optional in Git 2.56. The Makefile says so directly, and it stays optional until Git 3.0. The history command itself is plain C, so skipping Rust doesn't remove it. The build took about seven and a half minutes, then tripped at the very last step on msgfmt: not found — a missing translations tool. Cosmetic: the binary was already built, and ./git --version answered git version 2.56.0.

One thing to know before you copy those flags: NO_CURL=1 means this build can't talk HTTP. For this test that doesn't matter: everything happens on local repositories. If you need to clone over HTTPS, build with the headers installed instead.

The comparison, done properly

The original comparison, by Alex Georgiev, published November 13, is a clean piece of work, and I copied its method exactly so the numbers mean something side by side. Fresh repository: one root commit, one target commit to drop, then N descendant commits, each touching a shared file and its own file so the replay has real diff work to do. Clone it bare twice, so both methods start from byte-identical history.

  • Old way: add a linked worktree off the bare repo, run git rebase --onto to skip the target commit, remove the worktree.
  • New way: run git history drop directly against the bare repo. No worktree at all.

Three trials per size. And after every run, I compared the resulting tree hash of main between the two methods. If the trees don't match, the speed means nothing.

My numbers

Descendant commits Rebase (avg of 3) history drop (avg of 3) Speed-up
20 0.193s 0.034s 5.6×
100 0.810s 0.139s 5.8×
400 2.258s 0.325s 6.9×

Every run finished cleanly, and all nine tree comparisons matched exactly. The command does the same work, correctly, in about a sixth of the time.

Now put his numbers next to mine:

Descendant commits His rebase His history drop His speed-up
20 1.418s 0.035s 40.7×
100 7.121s 0.092s 77.5×
400 26.525s 0.362s 73.2×

Look at the right-hand column first. His history-drop times and mine are nearly the same: 0.035s vs 0.034s, 0.092s vs 0.139s, 0.362s vs 0.325s. The new command takes about a third of a second to replay 400 commits, on either machine.

Now look at the rebase column. His rebase took 26.5 seconds for 400 commits. Mine took 2.3. His baseline was ten times slower than mine, and the whole 40–77× headline is made of that difference. The ratio is a property of two machines, not of the command.

Why is his rebase so slow? I can't see his machine, so I won't guess at the cause: disk speed, filesystem, background load, any of those could do it. What I can say is what his own breakdown showed: the worktree setup he suspected was only 26 milliseconds of a 25-second run. The time goes into rebase cherry-picking each commit one at a time, updating the index and the working tree for every single one, even though nobody will ever look at those intermediate states. git history drop never touches a working tree at all — it works on the objects directly. That's the real mechanism, and it holds on my machine too. It just buys you 6× here instead of 70×, because rebase was never that slow here to begin with.

So is the 40–77× claim wrong?

Not wrong. Measured, on his machine, with a published method and matching tree hashes. But it's not a property of the command. If your rebase is already fast, expect single digits. If your rebase is slow — a big repo on a slow disk, hundreds of commits to replay — expect the headline numbers, or better.

The honest way to think about it: git history drop replays 400 commits in about a third of a second, on any machine. Rebase takes however long rebase takes on yours. Measure that, and you'll know your own speed-up.

What else the command does differently

Two things from his write-up are worth carrying over, because they change how you'd use it. Both checked by him directly, not by me.

First, one history drop updates every branch that descends from the dropped commit, not just the one you're standing on. A plain rebase rewrites only your current branch; a second branch past the same commit needs a second rebase. Here, both moved in a single run.

Second, it doesn't run hooks. He put a post-rewrite hook in a test repo and the drop never fired it, while the same hook fired immediately under rebase. If anything in your setup depends on post-rewrite: a notification, a cache update, a linter — switching a script to this command will silently stop that from happening. The man page says hooks aren't run "at the current point in time," which reads like a warning that it may change, not a promise.

And the refusals are clean: dropping the root commit or a merge commit fails immediately with a clear error and leaves nothing behind. A drop that would conflict during replay also fails all-or-nothing. No half-finished state, no conflict markers, no directory to clean up. Compare that with an interactive rebase hitting the same conflict, which stops mid-sequence with a dirty working tree. The man page calls this a design limitation — history rewrites aren't meant to be stateful operations — but from where I'm standing, a command that refuses to start a job it can't finish is a feature.

The catch, stated plainly

The man page marks the whole command experimental: "THIS COMMAND IS EXPERIMENTAL. THE BEHAVIOR MAY CHANGE." It has four subcommands: drop, fixup, reword, split — and I only tested drop. It isn't in any stable release your distribution ships yet, so today it means building from source. And until you've checked your hook dependencies, don't swap it into a script that other people rely on.

But for the job it was built for: dropping a commit from a bare repository, the kind of cleanup you do on a shared repo or a long-lived integration branch — it's the right tool. No throwaway clone, no worktree dance, a third of a second for 400 commits, and the trees come out identical.

My speed-up was 6×. His was 70×. The command was the same. Measure yours.

Sources

  • The claim and the method: Git 2.56's history drop command replays commits 40 to 77 times faster than rebase (Nov 13, 2026) — all of his figures above are his, quoted from that post
  • Git 2.56.0 source: git-2.56.0.tar.gz, mirrors.edge.kernel.org; release date September 28, 2026, per the same post
  • All of my timings, tree hashes and build notes: my own runs this morning, evidence in runs/git-256-history-drop/ (benchmark log, averages, build notes)

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: I Sorted Two Million Rows to Keep Ten
articles.description: A leaderboard endpoint that returns ten rows was allocating 56 MB to do it. A bounded PriorityQueue min-heap took it to 568 bytes, with real best-of-five numbers.
articles.body_html:
A leaderboard endpoint I wrote returns the ten highest-scoring players, and for a while I never thought about it twice. Ten rows out, done. Then it started showing up in our gen0 collection graphs during traffic spikes, which made no sense to me, because the response is ten rows. The allocation counter disagreed, and that counter has never once flattered me.

Here's the line that did it, more or less:

var top = players
    .OrderByDescending(p => p.Score)
    .Take(10)
    .ToList();

It reads exactly like what I want. Sort by score, take ten. The problem is the order of operations under the hood. OrderByDescending doesn't know I only want ten until Take shows up later in the chain, so it buffers every player into an internal array first, then sorts enough of it to hand ten back. To return ten rows, it holds all of them at once. On a small table nobody notices. On two million rows it's a very different graph.

Measuring it instead of guessing

I didn't want to argue from a hunch, so I wrote the smallest honest version I could. Two million rows of (id, score), built once up front so the data itself doesn't land on the scorecard. Then the top ten computed two ways, each wrapped in a best-of-five loop with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() and a checksum so a wrong answer couldn't sneak through.

The LINQ version printed this:

OrderByDescending().Take(K)      56,000,560 bytes    ~43 ms

Fifty-six megabytes to keep ten rows. The number came back byte-for-byte identical on every run, which is what you'd expect from something whose cost is "buffer N, sort N."

Keeping only the ten you care about

The fix is to never hold more than ten rows in the first place. A min-heap capped at K does exactly that: the smallest of the current top ten sits at the root, so any new row only has to beat that root to earn a spot. PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> has shipped since .NET 6 and it has the one method that makes this clean, EnqueueDequeue, which pushes a new item and pops the smallest in a single rebalance.

var heap = new PriorityQueue<Row, double>(K);
foreach (var r in rows)
{
    if (heap.Count < K)
        heap.Enqueue(r, r.Score);
    else if (r.Score > heap.Peek().Score)
        heap.EnqueueDequeue(r, r.Score);
}

Most rows never make it past the Peek() check. One comparison against the current tenth-best, and they're gone. The heap never grows beyond ten entries, so there's nothing to buffer and nothing for gen0 to clean up afterward. Here's the same two approaches side by side, best-of-five in a cloud container with workstation GC. This isn't a lab, so I care about the ratio, not the absolute milliseconds:

OrderByDescending().Take(K)              56,000,560 bytes    ~43 ms
Bounded PriorityQueue (min-heap of K)           568 bytes     ~6 ms

From fifty-six megabytes to five hundred and sixty-eight bytes, and quicker on the clock on top of it. I'd half expected the time to come out close, since LINQ does partial-sort the top of the buffer rather than sorting all two million. But buffering two million structs and running them through a comparer still costs you, and the heap just... doesn't do that.

When I'd leave the LINQ line alone

Most of the time I'd leave it alone, and I want to be clear about that. If your table has a few thousand rows, fifty-six megabytes becomes a few kilobytes and none of this matters. The LINQ version is shorter, it's obvious to the next person, and obvious code is worth real money. I only reach for the heap when K is tiny next to N and the thing runs hot. The whole win comes from that gap: ten out of two million is enormous leverage, ten out of thirty is nothing. And once K creeps close to N, you're basically sorting anyway, so just sort.

One sharp edge worth knowing: the heap gives you the top ten, but not in sorted order. The root is the smallest of the ten, not the largest. If you need them ranked, drain the heap and reverse, which is cheap because it's only ten items. I forgot that the first time and handed back a leaderboard sorted the wrong way, which is a fun bug to explain.

The full runnable sample

Dropping this in a file and running dotnet run -c Release reproduces the numbers. Tweak N and K at the top to find where the heap stops being worth it.

using System.Diagnostics;

const int N = 2_000_000;
const int K = 10;

var rng = new Random(20261114);
var rows = new Row[N];
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    rows[i] = new Row(i, rng.NextDouble() * 1000.0);

Console.WriteLine($"N = {N:N0} rows, K = {K}\n");

Measure("OrderByDescending().Take(K)", () =>
{
    var top = rows.OrderByDescending(r => r.Score).Take(K).ToList();
    return Checksum(top);
});

Measure("Bounded PriorityQueue (min-heap of K)", () =>
{
    var heap = new PriorityQueue<Row, double>(K);
    foreach (var r in rows)
    {
        if (heap.Count < K)
            heap.Enqueue(r, r.Score);
        else if (r.Score > heap.Peek().Score)
            heap.EnqueueDequeue(r, r.Score);
    }

    var top = new List<Row>(K);
    while (heap.Count > 0) top.Add(heap.Dequeue());
    top.Reverse();
    return Checksum(top);
});

static double Checksum(List<Row> top)
{
    double sum = 0;
    foreach (var r in top) sum += r.Score;
    return sum;
}

static void Measure(string label, Func<double> run)
{
    run();
    GC.Collect();
    GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
    GC.Collect();

    long bestBytes = long.MaxValue;
    double bestMs = double.MaxValue;
    double checksum = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    {
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        checksum = run();
        sw.Stop();
        long allocated = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before;

        if (allocated < bestBytes) bestBytes = allocated;
        if (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds < bestMs) bestMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
    }

    Console.WriteLine($"{label,-42} {bestBytes,14:N0} bytes   {bestMs,7:F1} ms   (checksum {checksum:F2})");
}

readonly record struct Row(int Id, double Score);

Have you got a top-N query sitting in a hot path somewhere? Check what it allocates before you assume it's fine. Mine looked harmless for months.

— still benchmarking the ten rows nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: One Month After the Hackathon: Why My 4-Service App Stopped Working (and What @mansio Caught in the Verifiers)
articles.description: What breaks a month after a hackathon, and what a fellow DEV writer caught in the verifiers.   TL;DR:...
articles.body_html:
What breaks a month after a hackathon, and what a fellow DEV writer caught in the verifiers.

TL;DR: A month after shipping README Clew 2, I opened it up and every scan failed. Nothing was wrong with the deterministic verifiers or with Jev on Glasser. Instead, three small operational traps lined up at once: an expired 30-day GitHub token on a tool that only reads public repos, a rotated Claude Haiku key scoped only to Development in Vercel, and a substring bug that fellow DEV writer Mikhail (@mansio) found and fixed in PR #2.

In October I built README Clew 2 for the AdaL "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon. It checks whether a public JavaScript or TypeScript repo's README matches its code, sorting every checkable line into four buckets: Contradicted, Missing, Unverifiable, and Verified.

The core rule of the build is that models never decide what is true:

Job Who does it
Split the README into lines and settle obvious headings/badges Deterministic code rules
Label what kind of claim a prose line makes (command, dependency, env var, file/URL) Jev (jev-1.13.0) via Glasser, gated at 0.8 confidence
Decide Verified, Contradicted, or Missing Five deterministic code verifiers
Write a two-sentence plain-English summary from the counts Claude Haiku (claude-haiku-5-5), fail-open

When you wire that many moving parts together (AdaL, Jev, Glasser, Haiku, GitHub, and Vercel) and come back a month later to a red SCAN FAILED banner, it is hard to tell at first glance which piece broke.

Here is what was actually wrong, and the two fixes that came out of it.

1. When "javascript" hides "ava": @mansio's PR #2

Before I even got to the deployment keys, Mikhail (@mansio) had opened and landed PR #2, the project's first external code contribution.

Mikhail was testing README Clew 2 against real repositories and noticed something strange on sindresorhus/yocto-queue. The repo uses ava as a test runner, and the README never mentions ava. The coverage verifier should have flagged ava in the Missing bucket. Instead, it stayed silent.

Why? Because the README contained a link to Mozilla's documentation:

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Iteration_protocols

And inside the word javascript, in lowercase, sits the three-letter substring ava.

Our coverage check was using a plain substring match:

// Before: any substring match counted as "mentioned in the README"
