if (readme.includes(name.toLowerCase())) continue;

Even worse, the same substring check lived in the dependency verifier's prose guard (inCodeContext), which checks whether a candidate package name appears on an install line. A short name like can inside npm i canvas-parser or lodash inside npm i lodash-es could bypass the prose guard and reach Contradicted, the exact false positive the guard was built to prevent.

The fix

Mikhail replaced both substring checks with a single whole-token rule, mentionsWord(), bounded by npm's own package name characters (A-Za-z0-9_-) plus @ and /:

export function mentionsWord(text, name) {
  if (!name) return false;
  const esc = name.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&');
  return new RegExp(`(?<![A-Za-z0-9_@/-])${esc}(?![A-Za-z0-9_-])`, 'i').test(text);
}

With that in place:

  • We use ava. and Tests run with \ava. still count as real mentions.
  • mozilla.org/.../javascript/... no longer hides ava.
  • npm i lodash-es no longer treats lodash as an installed package claim.

Mikhail shipped the fix with a 27-case test matrix and verifier controls in tests/mentions-word.test.js, matching the repo's file-size cap and offline test rules on the first try. If you have not read his engineering field notes on DEV (like The Dataset Was Lying: 4 of 6 "False" Facts Were True), go read him.

2. The 30-day time bomb: sending an expired token to a public API

Once Mikhail's PR was merged, I still had a live site that refused to scan.

Every click on SCAN returned HTTP 502:

{"error":{"code":"github_forbidden","message":"GitHub returned HTTP 401"}}

The ironic part: README Clew 2 only scans public repositories. It makes 4 metadata calls to api.github.com per scan and fetches the files from raw.githubusercontent.com. You do not even need a GITHUB_TOKEN for low-volume public reads (GitHub allows 60 unauthenticated REST calls per hour per IP, or 15 full scans per hour).

During the October hackathon, I had added a 30-day GitHub Personal Access Token so repeated test scans wouldn't hit the unauthenticated rate limit. Thirty days passed, the token expired, and lib/github.js kept sending Authorization: Bearer <expired_token> on every request.

GitHub allows requests with no Authorization header, but immediately rejects requests carrying an expired Authorization header with 401 Bad credentials. Because step 1 threw a GithubError, the pipeline stopped before Jev or Haiku ever ran.

The 4-line fix

First, I removed the expired GITHUB_TOKEN from Vercel. Second, we hardened lib/github.js so that if an expired token is ever present in .env or server environment variables and GitHub answers 401, the client drops the authorization header from the shared headers object and retries unauthenticated:

if (res.status === 401 && headers?.authorization) {
  delete headers.authorization; // expired or bad token: public repos work without it
  return request(url, { fetchImpl, headers, as });
}

Because headers is shared across the 4 metadata calls in fetchRepo(), dropping headers.authorization on the first 401 means the remaining 3 calls go straight out without the bad token.

3. Silent fail-open + Vercel environment scopes

The last piece was Claude Haiku. By design, Haiku is fail-open in README Clew 2: if the summary call fails or times out, the report still renders in full and the clew mascot falls back to a fixed one-line summary per mood.

My October Anthropic key had also been rotated. When I added the new ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in Vercel, two classic traps bit me at the same time:

  1. The new key was scoped to Development in Vercel, while Production and Preview still held the 34-day-old key.
  2. Vercel environment variable changes only take effect on the next deployment.

Running vercel env ls made the split visible right away:

Variable Environment Created
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (new) Development Today
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (old) Production, Preview 34d ago
GLASSER_API_KEY Production, Preview, Development 34d ago

Overriding ANTHROPIC_API_KEY across all three environments (Production, Preview, Development) and running vercel --prod brought the Haiku summary and bucket notes back on the first scan. Meanwhile, Glasser and Jev (jev-1.13.0) never missed a beat: all 4 batched calls completed in 1.37 seconds for about half a cent ($0.0055), with $10.80 of the original hackathon balance still untouched.

Related reading on DEV

Two posts from the community hit the exact operational edges from today's debugging session:

  • ["Invalid API key" or undefined env vars on Vercel: how to fix it] by @unbreakkit walks through how environment variable scopes (Production vs Preview vs Development) and missing redeploys cause 401 Invalid API key errors on Vercel even after you paste a fresh key.
  • [Your AI Agent Runs for Hours. Its GitHub Token Might Not.] by @__be2942592 looks at what happens when code assumes a GitHub token in the environment is valid forever instead of handling 401 expiration explicitly.

Try it

  • Live page: readme-clew-2.vercel.app (click USE DEMO REPO, then SCAN)
  • Source and 478 offline tests: github.com/earlgreyhot1701D/readme-clew-2

Thank you again to Mikhail (@mansio) for finding the substring bug on a real repo and shipping a clean, well-tested fix.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide. I build the Clew Suite, a set of civic tech tools for making complex systems easier to inspect. That is the lens I am writing from.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

articles.title: I built a racing sim that runs in a browser tab
articles.description: im racing usually starts with a big download and a decent PC. I wanted one you could open from a...
articles.body_html:
im racing usually starts with a big download and a decent PC. I wanted one you could open from a link.

That's LibreCorsa. It runs in the browser and it's open source. There are 2026-style open-wheelers, GT3s, a prototype and a road car, more than a dozen circuits, AI races, ghosts, rain and online races. You can drive it with a keyboard, a gamepad, a touch screen or a steering wheel. If you'd rather watch first, there's a 40-second trailer.

I'm building it on my own. It's a little over 800 commits since mid-October, and a few parts turned out much more interesting than I expected.

500 Hz, whatever your screen does

If the physics depends on frame rate, a 144 Hz monitor gives you more grip than a 60 Hz laptop. In a racing game you notice that within a lap.

So the simulation moves in fixed 2 ms steps (500 Hz), and each step splits into four 0.5 ms substeps for the tyres and suspension. The screen renders at whatever rate it can, and the sim catches up in whole steps. Stripped down, it's the classic loop:

const STEP = 0.002; // 500 Hz
let acc = 0;

function frame(dt: number) {
  acc = Math.min(acc + dt, 0.1); // a long hitch doesn't turn into a death spiral
  while (acc >= STEP) {
    sim.step(STEP); // four 0.5 ms substeps inside
    acc -= STEP;
  }
  render(sim.state);
}

One detail I didn't see coming: your steering input arrives once per frame, but a frame can run three physics steps or none. So each change is spread across the steps that frame actually runs, the way a real wheel turns, instead of landing all at once on the first one.

Does it hold? I run the same three-second launch at 30, 60, 144 and 240 fps, and the car ends within 0.3 km/h and 0.2 m every time. The test suite runs it at two frame rates and fails if they disagree.

Tyres are most of the work

The tyre is a Pacejka-style slip curve with combined slip, load sensitivity and carcass relaxation. Then it gets complicated. Each tyre tracks inner, middle and outer temperatures, and those move the grip window. Pressure follows the ideal gas law and changes how stiff the carcass is. Tyres wear. In the rain the road carries a water film that builds and drains, the cars dry the racing line first, and wets clear water up to a depth before they aquaplane.

The ground under the tyre mattered more than I thought. With one ground sample per wheel, a kerb's step edge gets hit at a point instead of rolled over. Each tyre now takes five samples across its contact patch (centre, both ends, both edges) and folds them into one height and slope.

There are two vehicle models. The default car has a planar chassis with sprung heave, pitch and roll. The others run a full 6-DOF rigid body with suspension built from hardpoints, so camber, bump steer and anti-dive come out of the geometry instead of numbers I typed in. On those cars the steering torque is the front tyres' moment about the kingpin axes. That's what a wheel actually pushes back with.

Checking it against a real car

When you're the only tester, tuning by feel only goes so far. I have about 24 minutes of MoTeC logs from a real GT3 Evo at Valencia, so the sim's GT3 runs the same manoeuvres: sustained cornering, braking and full-throttle acceleration at each speed, plus the gearing and the understeer gradient.

Right now every point sits within −13 % to +17 % of the logs. Not great, not terrible. The validation page is generated from the sim's own code with one command, and it has a section for where the sim is wrong. CI fails the build if a point leaves its band, and the last physics rework pushed one of them out.

Steering wheels in a browser

Steering, pedals and buttons were the easy part. If your OS sees the wheel as a game controller, the Gamepad API sees it too.

Force feedback is not easy. Chrome and Edge have WebHID, so a page can talk to a wheel base directly, and bases that speak the standard USB HID PID force-feedback reports can be driven with nothing installed. Plenty of popular wheels don't speak it. Logitech's force feedback is proprietary, for one. For those there's a small Windows helper that talks DirectInput and listens on localhost.

Where it stands: the one wheel I've tested, a MOZA R9, connects and steers over WebHID, but I haven't confirmed force feedback on it yet. It's marked experimental. If you have a different wheel, there's a wheel report form on GitHub and I'd love to see it filled in.

Racing people without paying for servers

Multiplayer is peer-to-peer over WebRTC. You host a room and send the link, or a friend types a 6-character code. If you want zero servers, there's a manual offer/answer copy-paste with nothing in between. Two tabs on the same machine can also race each other, which made testing a lot less lonely.

On the live site a small Cloudflare Worker does the rest. It pairs players, hands out relay servers for networks that block a direct link, keeps the leaderboards, and starts an open race every 20 minutes on the week's circuit and car. If nobody shows up, you race the AI.

Half a gigabyte, hosted for free

The game is a static Next.js export on Cloudflare, which is great until a circuit model is bigger than the asset store's 25 MiB per-file limit. Those files sit in an R2 bucket instead. The Worker answers any path that has no static file from R2, at the same URL, so the game never knows.

Car models are meshopt-compressed when the site builds. The default car drops from 16 MB to 6 MB, which matters when the first thing a player sees is a loading screen.

Hosting costs nothing at the moment. I'd like to keep it that way.

Licences, and why the repo is small

The code is MIT. The 3D models and sounds come from a lot of different authors with their own licences, and some are non-commercial. So LibreCorsa has no ads and nothing for sale. There's a Buy Me a Coffee link and that's it.

It's also why the repository carries only one circuit, RISE Motordrome, and the 2026 prototype car. Everything else is served on the site for playing there. A clone still gives you a working game with those two, and there's a guide for porting your own cars locally.

What's rough

VR works through WebXR, but it's a work in progress. Force feedback in the browser is experimental. Circuits converted from community 3D models have less trustworthy surfaces than the hand-built ones. And the handling is tuned by one person, which is exactly why I want other people driving it.

Try it

It's at librecorsa.org, and the code is on GitHub. Tell me how it drives, especially on a gamepad or a wheel I don't have, and how it runs on your machine.

LibreCorsa is an independent fan project. It isn't affiliated with Formula 1, the FIA, or any team or circuit.

articles.title: I put twelve 3D guests on our wedding website instead of writing "smart casual" (no 3D library)
articles.description: Shani and I get married in March 2027, in the highlands of South Africa. Every wedding website I...
articles.body_html:
Shani and I get married in March 2027, in the highlands of South Africa. Every wedding website I looked at had the same dress-code section: a line that says "smart casual" and leaves everyone guessing.

So I built ours by hand, and on the "What to wear" page I put twelve guests instead of a sentence.

boomslangchips.github.io

They show what to wear on each day of the weekend. They breathe, shift their weight, look around, fold their arms, glance at each other. You can drag one to turn them round, tap to step closer, and try the wedding colours on them.

There is no game engine and no 3D library behind it: about 250 KB of plain JavaScript and WebGL 1, plus one 760 KB file for the bodies. It runs on a phone.

How it fits together

File What it does
atelier-core.js Vectors, matrices, mesh building (tubes, shells, patches) and the WebGL renderer: skin, cloth, knit, denim, satin and hair shaders, a soft shadow map, the floor's reflection
atelier-body.js Reads the MakeHuman base mesh (CC0) in three body shapes, 163 bones and skin weights, and poses a body
atelier-cloth.js A small position-based cloth simulation for skirts and long hair, kept out of the body by the body's own cross-sections
atelier-figure.js One guest: body, face, hair, every garment cut round that body, shoes, accessories, and the arm poses
atelier-stage.js The stage: day tabs, dragging, the colour swatches, and each guest's little "mind" (breath, weight shifts, glances, blinks, smiles)

The hardest part was hands

Rendering was not the hard bit. Hands were.

A hand "on the hip" that floats a centimetre away looks wrong instantly. One that sinks into the hip looks worse. Folded hands that pass through each other are the first thing anyone notices. So each resting pose is solved: two-bone IK for the arm, then a small solver that places the palm against the surface it rests on, for every body shape.

The stage also watches its own frame time and does less on slow devices, and nothing moves at all if you have reduced motion turned on.

Honest limits

  • The guests stand in place: no walking.
  • Fingers keep one relaxed shape.
  • Creases at elbows and knees are drawn on the cloth, not simulated.
  • All faces are variations of one head.

The rest of the site

Our real site is private (it has our guest list on it), so I made a twin with a made-up couple and stock photos that you can click through: the invitation gate, a countdown, the weekend day by day, a drawn venue map, where to stay, an RSVP that knows who is on each invitation, and add-to-calendar.

👉 Demo: https://demo.wentzel.wedding (the invitation code is DEMO)
👉 3D guests, MIT licence: https://github.com/BoomslangChips/wedding-guests-3d

I wrote it with Claude Code over a few very long days. Happy to answer how any part works in the comments.

articles.title: I put a real LLM in my portfolio. It runs on your GPU, not my server.
articles.description: In-browser RAG with WebLLM and WebGPU, a hero animation that fires with every token, and the four mistakes I fixed on the way to Lighthouse 100.
articles.body_html:
Every AI-engineer portfolio says "I build with LLMs." I wanted mine to prove it in the first ten seconds.

So the chat box on my homepage has a button: Run a real LLM on your GPU. Click it and a 0.5B-parameter model downloads into your browser, boots on your graphics card through WebGPU, and answers questions about my work. No server. No API key. Nothing you type leaves your machine.

👉 Try it: rahul-agarwal.in (desktop Chrome or Edge works best)

Here's how it works, and the four things I got wrong before it worked well.

What happens when you click the button

  1. The page checks for WebGPU and whether your GPU supports 16-bit floats.
  2. It lazy-loads WebLLM from a CDN (none of this code ships until you ask for it).
  3. It downloads Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (about 270 MB, 4-bit quantised). Your browser caches it, so the second visit is instant.
  4. Every question runs a tiny retrieval step over my notes, then the model answers using only what was retrieved.
  5. Each generated token fires a pulse through the animated neural network behind the hero, so you can literally watch it think.

Loading the model (the part that's easier than you'd expect) 

const adapter = await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter();
const f16 = adapter.features.has('shader-f16');
const model = f16
  ? 'Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-q4f16_1-MLC'
  : 'Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-q4f32_1-MLC'; // fallback for GPUs without fp16

const webllm = await import('https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@mlc-ai/web-llm@0.2.86/+esm');
const engine = await webllm.CreateMLCEngine(model, {
  initProgressCallback: r => updateProgressBar(r.progress, r.text),
});

That's it. WebLLM exposes an OpenAI-style API, so streaming looks familiar:

const chunks = await engine.chat.completions.create({
  messages, stream: true, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 160,
});
for await (const c of chunks) {
  const token = c.choices[0]?.delta?.content || '';
  output.textContent += token;
  window.neural.fire(1); // light up the hero network
}

Two details matter: pin the CDN version (an unpinned import can change under you), and check for shader-f16 instead of assuming it. Plenty of laptop GPUs don't have it.

Grounding a 0.5B model with a 30-line RAG

A half-billion-parameter model knows nothing about me and will happily invent things. So it never answers from memory. Every question goes through a retrieval step first:

// Simplified from the real code, which also weights longer keywords higher
function retrieve(question) {
  const q = question.toLowerCase();
  return NOTES
    .map(note => ({ note, score: note.keys.filter(k => q.includes(k)).length }))
    .filter(x => x.score > 0)
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
    .slice(0, 2)
    .map(x => x.note);
}

const SYSTEM = `Answer in 1 to 3 short sentences using ONLY the notes provided.
If the notes don't contain the answer, say you don't know.
Never invent companies, numbers, dates or links.`;

The notes are a dozen short paragraphs I wrote (projects, stack, experience). Keyword scoring sounds crude next to embeddings, but with a dozen documents it's instant, deterministic and easy to debug. Under every answer the UI shows what it used:

Q: Where does he work now?
A: Rahul is the sole engineer at Aryan News Agency, where he builds and develops websites and apps.
↳ retrieved 1 note (intro) · 22 tokens in 2.8s · generated on your GPU

And the test I cared about most:

Q: What is his favourite food?
A: Rahul is not specifically known for his favorite food.

No hallucination. Low temperature plus a strict "only the notes" prompt does most of the work.

Four things I got wrong

1. The first answer took 28 seconds

The model loaded fine, but the first question sat there "thinking." WebGPU compiles its shaders lazily, on the first real inference. The fix is a throwaway warm-up generation while the progress bar is still visible:

await engine.chat.completions.create({
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }], max_tokens: 4,
});

Now the slow part happens during loading, where users expect waiting, not after they've asked a question.

2. A text animation wrecked my layout score

My headline "decodes" from random glyphs into the real text. It looked great, and it gave the page a Cumulative Layout Shift of 1.41 (anything above 0.25 is "poor"). Random glyphs have different widths, so the line re-wrapped about 60 times a second and shoved everything below it around.

The fix: wrap each word in an inline-block, lock it to its real width, scramble inside it, then unwrap.

for (const w of words) {
  w.span.style.display = 'inline-block';
  w.span.style.width = w.span.getBoundingClientRect().width + 'px';
}
// ...animate...then restore plain text nodes
words.forEach(w => w.span.replaceWith(document.createTextNode(w.text)));

Same effect, layout shift 0.00. One more catch: measure after document.fonts.ready, or you lock in the fallback font's widths.

3. My CDN was editing my HTML

I added a strict Content-Security-Policy (hash-based, no unsafe-inline). Locally: zero violations. In production: errors. My domain was proxied through Cloudflare in front of Vercel, and Cloudflare was injecting its own inline scripts (analytics and bot detection) and rewriting my email address into an obfuscated link. That put an <a> inside my "copy email" <button>.

Switching the DNS records to "DNS only" removed the extra hop and the rewriting. The strict CSP went back on, and the page got faster. If you put a CDN in front of a platform that's already a CDN, check what it's adding to your pages.

4. Assuming everyone has WebGPU

Plenty of visitors (many phones, older browsers) can't run the model. The chat works without it: by default it streams pre-written answers token by token, clearly labelled as "scripted mode". The real model is opt-in, behind an explicit button that shows the download size. Nobody gets a 270 MB surprise on mobile data.

The numbers

Framework none: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript
HTML + CSS + JS over the wire ~37 KB gzipped
Lighthouse (desktop) 100 / 100 / 100 / 100
Lighthouse (mobile) 97 / 100 / 100 / 100
Mozilla Observatory A+
Model download (optional) ~270 MB once, then cached

No React, no build step. Every heavy thing (the model, the runtime) loads only when someone asks for it, and every animation pauses when it scrolls off screen.

What I'd do differently

  • A 0.5B model is a demo, not a product. It's grounded and fast, but its phrasing is sometimes clumsy. With a bigger download budget, a 1.5B model is noticeably better.
  • Keyword retrieval doesn't scale. Past a few dozen notes I'd switch to small embeddings computed in the browser.
  • First load is the real UX problem. On a slow connection the download takes minutes. The progress bar helps, but caching the model with a service worker before anyone clicks would be smarter.

Have you shipped anything that runs a model fully client-side? I'd love to hear what you used and what broke. Drop it in the comments 👇

I'm Rahul, an AI engineer in Bengaluru who builds tools that ship. More of my work is at rahul-agarwal.in, and the code is on GitHub.

articles.title: I Built a Free Browser Shooter Set in a Pakistani Old-City Bazaar
articles.description: A free desktop-browser shooter set in Purana Shehr, a Pakistani old-city bazaar. What's in the game, what it needs, and how to try it.
articles.body_html:
I built a shooter set in a Pakistani bazaar, and it runs in a desktop browser. There is nothing to install.

The game is called Operation Androon. A match is 8 v 8 team deathmatch against computer-controlled soldiers, and the first team to 50 eliminations wins. The map is Purana Shehr: an old-city bazaar with a clock tower, shop signs in Urdu, decorated trucks, rickshaws, fruit stalls, and a haveli courtyard.

I am a lead full-stack engineer in Lahore, and the founder of MyLeadBots. On my site, azeemshafeeq.com, I describe these games as side projects where I learn game development. Androon is one of them. This post is a clear look at what is in the game, what it needs, and what it is not.

The place: Purana Shehr

Purana Shehr is a fictional Pakistani old-city bazaar. The name is Urdu for "old city," and the map is built around details you would expect to see in that kind of place, not around a generic arena with a different coat of paint.

The square is marked by a clock tower. Shop signs are in Urdu. Decorated trucks sit in the lanes. There are rickshaws, fruit stalls, and a haveli courtyard. Lanes are narrow enough that a firefight can move from the street into a doorway and then up a stairwell.

You can go inside buildings, climb the stairs, and fight from the rooftops. That matters for how a match feels. A rooftop gives you a line of sight over the bazaar; a shop interior gives you cover and a tighter fight. The map plays as a small district: streets, interiors, and rooftops, not a flat deathmatch pad.

Civilians shelter in the shops. Hitting one costs your team points. The bazaar is not only scenery. If you spray through a storefront, you can lose ground even if you win the gunfight.

I will not call the graphics photorealistic, and I will not call them console-quality. This is a browser game, built for the web, and the honest description is that it is a stylized place you can move through, not a simulation of a real street.

How a match works

A match is straightforward:

  • You play 8 v 8, on a team, alongside and against bots.
  • The first team to 50 eliminations wins.
  • Eight weapons unlock as you get kills.
  • Grenades are in the mix, and a 5-kill streak calls in an airstrike.
  • You can switch between first-person and third-person views.

The bots are the other team and your teammates. I am not calling this multiplayer. You are not dropping into a match with other people over the network. You are playing a team deathmatch against computer-controlled soldiers in your browser.

The weapon unlocks give the match a short arc. You start with less, and you earn more as you get kills. The airstrike on a 5-kill streak is a payoff for a run that stays clean. None of that changes the basic rule: first to 50.

There is also a Veteran difficulty, if you want a harder pass through the same map.

First-person and third-person are both there because the bazaar rewards both ways of looking. First-person is tighter in a doorway or on a stair. Third-person makes it easier to see the edge of a rooftop or the corner of a lane before you step into it. You can switch as you play.

If you have played classic military shooters, the loop will feel familiar: a team deathmatch, a small set of weapons, a map you learn by running it. Operation Androon is an original game. The setting is the part worth naming clearly: a Pakistani old-city bazaar, not a stand-in for somewhere else.

What it runs on, and what it does not

Operation Androon is free. It runs in a desktop browser. There is no download and nothing to install.

It needs a laptop or PC with a mouse and keyboard. It does not work on phones. I am stating that up front because a browser game is easy to open on a phone, and this one will not play well there. The controls assume a mouse and a keyboard.

The first load is about 42 MB. On a new device, or a slower connection, that first visit can take a moment. After that, you are in the bazaar.

Those limits are worth stating clearly, not hiding in a footnote. A desktop browser can hold a small 3D district, interiors, and a team of bots. A phone screen and a touch overlay are a different game, and this is not that game.

Where this sits in my work

Most of my professional work is web and AI products. MyLeadBots is a SaaS tool I built for small web agencies and freelance website builders: it finds local businesses from Google Maps, checks their public presence, and prepares reviewable proof before a pitch. I also ship other production work, which I keep on azeemshafeeq.com.

The games are how I learn a different kind of building. Androon is the bazaar shooter. Next to it I have been working on Morrow, a 3D night-city district that also runs in a desktop browser, and Sands of the Lost Kingdom, a fantasy adventure whose first chapter is a macOS preview built in Godot. I am not packing those into this article. I mention them only so the context is honest: Androon is a side project, and it is one of a small set.

I am writing this as a show-and-tell, not as a launch with user numbers or a claim about how it plays for other people. I have not published player counts, scores, or reviews, and I will not invent any here.

Credit

The soldier model is "PAKISTAN soldier – PAK ARMY" by Abdullah5007 on Sketchfab, licensed under CC BY 4.0, then rigged and modified for the game. The licence requires attribution, so I am putting it here in the article as well as on my site.

If you want to try it

If you want to play Operation Androon, DM me on X @azeem_sh123 and I will send the link. Use a laptop or PC with a mouse and keyboard.

I would rather hear what you notice about the map than a generic "cool game" note. The useful feedback is specific: a lane that is hard to read, a rooftop that works, a shop you expected to be able to enter, a Pakistani detail that is missing.

If you were adding one thing to a bazaar map like this, what would you put in next: another street, another weapon, or something quieter, like a tea stall you can actually walk into?

articles.title: Keep client customisations out of your product: an iframe sandbox
articles.description: Every client wants something different, and AI makes it cheap to build. I built a zero-dependency browser sandbox so those customisations stay out of
articles.body_html:
Every client wants something slightly different, and AI just made those differences cheap to build. I think that changes how products get shaped, so I built a sandbox for it: sandbox-environment, Apache-2.0, zero runtime dependencies, on JSR as @panth977/sandbox.

I'm Panth Patel. I work on backends and developer tooling, and this is the argument behind the library more than a tour of it.

From product to framework

Many companies went from solutions to SaaS: stop building one thing per client and sell one thing to everyone. My view is that the next move runs from product to framework. With AI around, and with less organised sectors coming online, each client will have different needs and will expect them met.

Those needs have to live somewhere. The easy answer is to have AI stitch them into your app. It works for a while. Then your product code holds every client's special case, and each customisation is a product change with a product release.

The better principle is a line. Framework code on one side, client customisation on the other, and a sandbox as that line. Yes, you'll probably still use AI to write what goes inside it. That is fine. What changes is where the code lands.

It gives you two things. A customisation that needs no product code change can ship in hours instead of weeks. And if the client has a tech team of their own, you can hand them the sandbox and let them maintain it.

What it looks like

A customisation is an artifact: a mini-app mounted in a slot of your app.

import { mount, scopes, confirm, audit } from "jsr:@panth977/sandbox/host";

mount(document.getElementById("slot")!, {
  artifact,
  api: {
    devices: {
      list: (q) => http.get("/devices", { params: q }),   // uses YOUR token
    },
  },
  middleware: [
    audit((e) => log.push(e)),
    scopes({ "devices.list": "devices:read" }, granted),
  ],
});

Inside the artifact, the code only sees the API you passed in:

import { host } from "@panth977/sandbox/artifact";
const rows = await host.devices.list();

Your frontend is its backend. The call crosses a typed bridge, runs in your app with the viewer's permissions, and comes back. Streams, callbacks, cancellation and errors cross it too.

Where the boundary comes from

I didn't write a security model. I used the browser's. Each artifact runs in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> with an opaque origin, so it has no access to your DOM, cookies, localStorage or tokens. A strict CSP closes the network unless the artifact's manifest asks and the host allows it. Scopes, confirm-before-destructive, rate limits, an audit trail and dry runs are middleware, a line each.

The threat model is written down in SECURITY.md. The artifact is untrusted, and the host and its API are trusted. Two things are out of scope: an artifact wasting its own frame, and anything your API chooses to allow. The sandbox stops the code from reaching around your API. You still have to design that API with care.

Writing artifacts in the browser

A sandbox nobody can write for doesn't help. So the package includes the tools:

  • A compiler that takes TypeScript, JSX and Svelte in the browser or a worker, with no bundler and no WASM. The same compiler runs in Node for CI.
  • mountDev: a Monaco editor with completions and go-to-definition, plus a live preview.
  • A UI kit, so artifacts look like part of your app.

Hosts can be plain JS, Svelte or Angular, tested in CI in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, with Angular as far back as 15. Artifacts can be plain JS, React, Preact or Svelte 5. A React host should work through the custom element, but I haven't tested one in a real React app yet.

What's next

This release covers the frontend. The next one is a backend sandbox: write the code in any language, while the host keeps full control over the script and its security.

Where do client customisations live in your product today?
